chunks: We said: We had previously discussed in the chapter on the obligation of Imamate, where we indicated it, that the extension of his hand (peace be upon him) and the fear of his discipline were missed by the duty-bound (Mukallaf) only insofar as it pertains to them,
because they forced him into concealment by fearing him and not allowing him [to act], so the deficiency came from their own selves.

And that occurred in the manner of someone saying: 'He who does not attain knowledge of God Almighty during his period of obligation, his obligation is ugly/flawed,' because the favor of knowledge did not befall him, so his obligation ought to be considered flawed.

key_terms.الْمُكَلَّفِينَ: The duty-bound (those subject to religious obligations)

ai.seo_question: How does the Shia scholarly tradition justify the occultation of the Imam as a result of human action rather than divine neglect?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes the Imam's occultation not as a divine omission but as a consequence of the Mukallafin's own actions, specifically their fear and prevention of the Imam's active guidance. He employs the juristic concept of 'ugliness' (Qubh) in obligation to argue that since the Imam's presence is a divine favor (Lutf), its absence due to human agency does not invalidate the duty but rather shifts the cause of the resulting spiritual deficiency to the people themselves.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: Evil of belief in occultation of the Imam can be proved by stating that it removes hardships and hurdles from the duty-bound (Mukallaf), because by keeping away assistance of the Imam, which in fact is a divine favor, and in the same way, fear of people of being reprimanded by the Imam [if they commit disobedience] is not achieved.
Thus it is a breach of divine grace on the duty-bound (Mukallaf)
and that is why belief in occultation is evil.
